Article 79: Constitution of Parliament
There shall be a Parliament of India that consists of:
Two Houses:
Council of States (Rajya Sabha) - Upper House House of the People (Lok Sabha) - Lower House Lok Sabha (LS):
First sitting: 13 May 1952
Constituted on: 17 April, 1952
e is also known as the 'House of the People' (Hindi name adopted in 1954)
Members elected directly by the people.
Themes of New Parliament buildings: Lok Sabha: Peacock
Rajya Sabha (RS): First sitting: 13 May 1952
Constituted on: 3 April, 1952
e is also known as the 'Council of States' / 'Permanent House' (Hindi name adopted in 1954)
Also known as the 'House of Elders'
President is an integral part of Parliament because No Bill becomes law without his assent.
Article 80: Composition of Council of States (Rajya Sabha)
Total Members: 238 elected members
Maximum 250 ara 12 nominated by the President:
From the fields of— (LiSAS) i.e.
Literature, Science, Arts, Social
Present strength of RS: 245 (233 elected, 12 nominated)
5 seats are vacant for PoK, Aksai Chin, etc.

Members are indire- ctly elected by means of Proportional Represen- tation and Single Transferable Vote (STV)
Note: President to Nominated Members
Unequal representation in RS (based on population)
Election of RS members is borrowed from South Africa.
Nomination of RS members is taken from Ireland Article 81: Composition of House of the People (Lok Sabha)
Total Members: —— 530 from States
Present strength: 543 elected members.
2 Anglo Indians were nominated by President, this provision was abolished through 104 CA, 2019.
Representation in LS:
Directly elected by citizens.
Parity maintained among Inter and Intra States.
Q. Do you know why Lok Sabha has green carpet and Rajya Sabha has red Carpet?
Ans: Green colour represents that India is an agricultural land and people here elected from grassroots level.
Red colour represents royalty and symbolises the sacrifices done by the freedom fighters and the blood they shed to gain independence for India.
Article 82: Readjustment after Each Census Delimitation Commission established after every Census (10 years) to:
Divides constituencies based on population.
President of India appoints the Delimitation Commission in consultation with the ECI.
Important Delimitation Acts:
Delimitation Commission has been setup 4 times. 1st in 1952 Key Amendments:
42nd CA (1976): Seats were frozen based on 1971 Census until 2000.
84th CA (2001): Freeze on Delimitation Commission extended till 2026.
87th CA (2003): Minor adjustments, Delimitation according to 2001 Census.
"Delimitation" means the act or process of fixing limits or boundaries of territorial constituencies.
Article 83: Duration of Houses
Rajya Sabha:
Permanent body; not subject to dissolution.
1/3rd members retire every 2 years
Term of members of RS is 6 years.
Lok Sabha:
Tenure: 5 years.
42nd CA (1976) - Increased tenure of Lok Sabha to 6 Years.
44th CA (1978) - Restored Status Quo — Ante (i.e. to 5 years)
ie President authorized to dissolve Lok Sabha on the advice of PM.
Can be extended during national emergency (one year at a time).
Elections must be held within 6 months after the end of emergency.
The 12th LS had the shortest span in Indian history lasting only 13 months 4 days (from 10 March 1998 to 26 April 1999).

Must be a citizen of India.

Minimum required age: a particular state should be

Article 85: Sessions of Parliament, Prorogation, and Dissolution on the advice of Council of Ministers.
Parliamentary Sessions: (summoned by the President)
Budget Session: February to April end / May first
Monsoon Session: July-August / September
Winter Session: November / December
Note: Maximum gap between sessions cannot exceed 6 months.
Prorogation: Ends a session (by President).
Dissolution: Formal termination of the current Lok Sabha (by President) on the aid & advise of CoM.
Adjournment: Temporary break within a session where a sitting is terminated (by Presiding Officer).
Adjournment Sine die: by Presiding Officer Ends the session meeting without fixing a date for next session, happens just before prorogation.
The adjournment motionis introduced in the Parliament to draw the attention of the house to a definite matter of urgent public importance and needs the support of 50 members to be admitted.
Some other Parliamentary motion/Procedures:
Closure Motion: A motion moved by a member to cut short the debate on a matter before the house.
Call Attention Motion: It is introduced in Parliament by a member to call the attention of a minister on a matter of public importance.
Point of Order: It is raised when the proceedings of the house do not follow the normal rules of procedure. No debate is allowed on Point of Order.
Censure Motion No reason required
Reason must be stated
Can be moved against entire

Can be moved against an council only. individual, group, OT entire council To tests majority support To target for some specific (confidence) of LS in CoM. policies/actions If passed — resignation is If passed — no resignation mandatory required Types of Questions:
Starred: Oral question-answers, can have supplementary questions.
Unstarred: Required written answers, No Supplementary questions could follow.
Short Notice: 10 days prior notice should be given.
Routine of a session: 11AM: Session Starts
11 AM-12 PM: Question Hour
12-1 PM: Zero Hour
Question could also be asked to private members.
(A private member is the one who is not a minister.)
Zero Hour: Informal device to raise matter without any prior notice. It lasts until the agenda for the day is taken up.
Article 86: Right of President to Address and Send Messages
President can address either House or both Houses jointly.
President can send messages regarding pending Bills or other matters.
Article 87: Special Address by the President
President addresses both the Houses in two scenarios:
The first session after each general election.
The first session of each fiscal year.
It is also known as Motion of Thanks
Article 88: Rights of Ministers and Attorney General
Right to speak in either House but can vote only in that house of which they are a member.
Attorney General is not a member of either house but has the right to speak in LS/RS, without having Right to Vote.
Officers of Parliament:
Article 89: Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha
Chairman: Vice President of India (Ex-officio).
He is not a member of RS.
Deputy Chairman: Elected by Rajya Sabha.
Fulfills duties as the Acting Chairman in absence of the Chairman.
He is a member of RS.
While the Chairman is presiding the house, he is like any other member of the house.
Article 90: Vacation, Res ignation, Removal D Chairman of ott
Resignation: by writing to the Chairman.
Removal by Effective maj ority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha.
(Effective Majority = Maj ority of the total membership of house - Vacancies)
Article 91: Power/Duty of Deputy Chairman
Presides in absence of Chairman.
When Seats of Chairman and Deputy Chairman are vacant: then President can choose any member from the house to discharge duties of RS.
If the Chairman and Deputy Chairman, both are absent, then: one member of the Panel of Vice-Chairpersons, appointed by the Chairman, presides. (This is not explicitly mentioned in Constitution).
Article 92: Chairman and Deputy Chairman Not to Preside During their removal
They can participate in proceedings but cannot preside during their own removal resolution.
Like the speaker of the LS, the chairman of the RS does not vote in the first instance because he is not a member of the RS. He can only exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.
However, the Deputy Chairman of the RS being a member of the house can:
Vote in the first instance.
—> In case of equality of votes, also exercise a casting vote when presiding.
P.T, Usha: first woman to be appointed in the RS panel of Vice-Chairpersons.
Article 93: Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
Elected by Lok Sabha members by Simple Majority
First Speaker: Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar.
First Deputy Speaker: M.A. Ayyangar.
1st Female Speaker: Meira Kumar (15th Speaker).
The Speaker of the L.S. is the ex-officio president of the Indian Parliamentary Group (IGP).
The speaker is empowered to refer suo motu, any question of privilege for investigation.
Note: No Deputy Speaker appointed since 2019.
Article 94: Vacation, Resignation, Removal of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
Resignation: Speaker resigns to Deputy Speaker and vice- versa.
Removal: by Effective majority.
Speaker continues till a new Speaker is elected,
He does not immediately resign after the dissolution of LS and continue till the newly elected LS meets.
Date of election of Speaker is fixed by the President, and that of deputy speaker is fixed by speaker.
Article 95: Powers to Perform Duties
Deputy Speaker presides when Speaker is absent.
If the Seat is vacant: then President can choose any member to discharge the duties.
If the speaker and Deputy speaker, both are absent, then: one member of the Panel of Chairpersons, appointed by the Speaker presides.
Article 96: Speaker and Deputy Speaker Not to Preside During Their Removal.

They can participate but cannot preside while a motion for their removal is under discussion. (The Speaker's right to vote in the first instance is retained, but has no right to casting their vote in the case of tie.)
Note: Deputy speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker.
Article 97: Salaries and Allowances
Salaries of Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Speaker and Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha are decided by Parliament.
Article 98: Secretariat of Parliament
Each House has its separate secretarial staff.
Secretariat is appointed by the President on the advice of the Speaker of the LS and Chairman of RS.
Functions of the Cabinet Secretariat:
To ensure interministerial co-ordination — Management of major crisis — Monitoring policy implementation — Organizing agendas — Recording minutes.
Article 99: Oath or Affirmations by Members Every member of either House must take oath before taking his seat as administered by the President or a person appointed by him.
Protem Speaker:

Senior-most member appointed temporarily by President to administer oath to newly elected members of new Lok Sabha. As soon as the oath is administered the house selects Full time Speaker. First pro-tem speaker to be unanimously elected as the speaker of the Lok Sabha- Somnath Chatterjee.
Article 100: Voting in Houses and Quorum
100(1) The Chairman or Speaker shall not vote in the 1st instance but shall exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.
100(3) Quorum: Minimum 1/10th of total strength of House is required to carry on the proceedings.
100(4) If quorum is not met, house is adjourned by the presiding officer.
Article 101: Vacation of Seats
101(1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of Parliament.
101(2) No person can be a member of State Legislature and a member of Parliament.
101(3) Members can be disqualified as mentioned in Article 101(3A) A member can resign his seat to the Chairman or Speaker.
101(4) If member of either of the Houses of Parliament is absent without permission for a period of 60 days, the house may declare the seat vacant.
RPA: Representation of People Act, 1951
Jail for more than two years lead to disqualification.
Article 102: Disqualifications for Membership 102(1) A person shall be disqualified for membership if:
(a) He holds any office of profit under the Union or State Government.
(b) He is of unsound mind, as declared by a competent court.
(c) He is an undischarged insolvent.
(d) He is not a citizen of India.
(e) He voluntarily acquired citizenship of another country or allegiance to a foreign State.
102(2) Disqualification under 10th Schedule— Defection On the grounds of:
Independent members join any political party.
Nominated members join the political party after 6 months from the date of his nomination.
If he votes contrary to the direction of his party.
If the member voluntarily gives up the membership of the party on whose ticket he has been elected.
Exception: Merger when 2/3rd members leave and join other political party (91st CA, 2003), then there is no disqualification.
WHIP:
A whip is a direction issued by a political party to its members to vote in a particular manner in the house.
A member is disqualified if:
He/She votes against or abstains from the party whip
Without prior permission and
The act is not condoned within 15 days
Thus, the violation of whip leads to disqualification under the Anti-Defection Law.
Decision of the Speaker is final with regard to disqualification under defection.
Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachilhu Case: Judiciary can review the final decision of the Speaker in case of disqualification under Defection.

Article 103: Decision on Questions of Disqualification 103(1) Decision of the President shall be deemed final if question arises over disqualification of any member of the either house (other than defection).
103(2) President must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission before giving his final decision.
Article 104: Penalty for Sitting and Voting When Disqualified or before making an oath or affirmation under Article 99
If any person sits or votes knowing they are disqualified, a penalty of Rs. 500 per day is charged for the period he/she sat or voted.
Article 105: Powers, Privileges, and Immunities of Parliament Members 105(1) Freedom of speech in Parliament.
105(2) No proceedings in Parliament can be questioned in any court of law.
No MP liable for anything said or any vote given in Parliament.
105(3) MPs enjoy protection from civil arrest during a session and 40 days before and after the session (by parliamentary convention).
This protection does not apply to criminal arrest or preventive detention (Note: Protection of the President from criminal proceedings is under Article 361, not Article 105)
Article 106: Salaries and Allowances of Members
Parliament may by law fix salaries and allowances of members of both the Houses.
Article 107: Introduction and Passing of Bills 107(1) A Bill can originate in either House (LS or RS) except the Money bill.
107(2) A Bill passes if both Houses agree, with or without amendments.
107(3) Bill pending in Parliament does not lapse due to adjournment or prorogation of the session.
107(4) Bills lapsing after dissolution:
A Bill pending in Lok Sabha and not passed at the time of its dissolution lapses.
A Bill pending in the RS, which has not been passed by the LS shall not lapse on the dissolution of the LS.
Ordinary Bill Financial Bill
1 week prior notice should be given

Article 108: Joint Sitting of Both Houses Provision of 108(1) In case of a deadlock (disagreement · Jit sifting between both Houses), the President may · '* taken from Australia. summon a Joint Sitting.
A deadlock is created if:

(a) The bill is rejected by the other house; or (b) The houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments to be made in the bill; or (c) More than six months have lapsed since the date of reception of the Bill by the other House without it being passed.
108(2) Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over the Joint Sitting.
In his absence Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha presides.
In absence of both, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha presides (Chairman cannot preside the Joint sitting as he is not the member of either house).
Exceptions:
Money Bill and Constitutional Amendment Bill — No Joint Sitting allowed.
Simple majority is needed to pass the Bill (majority of members present and voting).
Joint Sitting follows the Rules of Lok Sabha Joint Sitting has happened 3 times till now:
Dowry Prohibition Bill, 1960
Banking Services Commission Bill, 1977
Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 2002
Article 109: Special Procedure for Money Bills 109(1) A Money Bill can only be introduced in Lok Sabha, Kabhi Kabhi Lagta hai on the recommendation of the Apun Hi Bhagwaan Hai President.
109(2) After a bill is passed to RS, it can: approve, suggest Lok Sabha in case of Money Bill amendments or take no action on the bill but it must give its response within 14 days.
109(3) Lok Sabha may accept or reject Rajya Sabha's suggestions.
If RS does not pass the bill within 14 days —It shall be deemed passed by both Houses.
Article 110: Definition of Money Bill
A Bill is a Money Bill if it contains only provisions related to:
(a) Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, regulation of any tax.
(b) Regulation of borrowings.
(c) Custody and audit of Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund (d) Appropriation of money out of Consolidated Fund.
(e) Declaring any expenditure as charged on Consolidated Fund.
(f) The receipt of money into the Consolidated Fund of India or the Public Account of India, or the custody or issue of such money.
Though the speaker's decision on a Money Bill is final it is subject to limited Judicial review as affirmed by the SC in the Aadhaar (K.S. Puttaswamy vs Union of India case 2018).
The Speaker of Lok Sabha certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not.
A Bill is not considered as a money bill if it provides:
For the imposition of fine/imposition or abolition of any tax by local Authority Article 111: Assent to Bills
After a bill is passed by both the Houses the bill is then presented to the President.
President may:
(a) Give assent — Bill becomes a law.
(b) Use its Veto power.
Veto Powers of the President (Negative Powers)
Absolute Veto: President rejects the Bill completely.
This veto was first used by Dr. Rajendra Prasad for PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954.
In 1991 R. Venkataraman exercised absolute veto over Parliamentary Salaries Bill.
Suspensive Veto: President returns the Bill for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again, assent is mandatory.
Not available in case of Money bill because it is already brought into the Parliament after the prior recommendation of the President.
Pocket Veto: No action taken by President. (No time limit to act.)
This veto was first used by Gyani Zail Singh for Indian Post Office (amendment) bill 1986.
24th CA provided that No Veto can be used in case of a Constitutional Bill.
Pocket of Indian President is deeper than the US president because no time limit is mentioned in constitution for Indian president to act on the bill. US President has to return in 10 days.
Article 112: Annual Financial Statement (Budget)
President shall cause to be
The term 'Budget' laid before both the Houses, a is not mentioned in statement of estimated receipts and the Constitution. expenditures.
The Indian Railway Budget was separated from the General Budget in 1924 based on the Acworth Committee report.
In 2017 the 92-year-old practice ended; then-Finance Minister Arun Jaitley presented the first merged Union Budget, ending separate railway budget presentations.
POLLEY, · Article 113: Procedure in Parliament with respect to Estimates.
No expenditure from Consolidated Fund of India be done except with the authorization by Parliament.
Estimates of Expenditure are divided into two parts:
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (not votable due to salaries of President, SC judges, etc.)
Made from the Consolidated Fund of India (subject to vote in Lok Sabha through Demands for Grants).
Only Lok Sabha has the right to vote on Demands for Grants. RS can only discuss it.
Demands for Grants are presented on behalf of the President.
Types of Funds in the Constitution 1. Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266(1))
All revenues received by Government of India
All money received in repayment of loans
Largest and most important fund
No money can be withdrawn without Parliamentary ED [SP OU approval (Appropriation Act)
Covers: Salaries, schemes, defense, etc.
2. Public Account of India (Article 266(2))
Money held by government as a banker/trustee
Includes: Provident Fund, Small savings, Deposits, etc.
No Parliamentary approval required for withdrawal
Government only acts as custodian 3. Contingency Fund of India (Article 267)
Fund for emergency/unforeseen expenditure
Controlled by President of India,
Operated by Finance Secretary on behalf of President
Requires post-facto approval of Parliament Article 114: Appropriation Bills
The Appropriation Bill is introduced to authorize the withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India.
No amendments or voting on the Appropriation Bill amounts — it is passed as a formality after Demands for Grants are voted.
Cut motions are moved during the voting on Demands for Grants to show the disapproval towards the Govt.
1. Policy Cut: Reduce the amount to 21, to criticize government policy.
2. Economy Cut: Reduce by a specified amount, to suggest savings.
3. Token Cut: Reduce by 2100, to raise a specific grievance.
Article 115: Supplementary, Additional, Excess grants
Supplementary grant: granted when the amount authorised by Parliament is found insufficient
Additional grant: granted for additional expenditure upon some new service.
Excess grant: It is granted when money has been spent on any service in excess of the amount granted to that service in the budget.
Article 116: Vote on Account, Votes of Credit, and Exceptional Grants Vote on Account:
Authorizes the government to withdraw funds from the Consolidated fund of India for essential, short-term expenditures.
It deals solely with the expenditure side of the budget.
Vote on Credit:
Financial grant given to the Executive from India's resources to meet urgent financial needs.
Details cannot be shared ordinarily in a budget.
It acts like a blank cheque given to the Executive by the Lok Sabha (LS).
Exceptional Grants:
Special provisions made by Parliament.
Used to meet specific expenses not covered under the regular budgetary allocation.
Stages in enactment of budget
Presentation Discussion Scrutiny by departmental committees Voting on demands for grants Passing of Appropriation bill Passing of Finance bill Article 117: Special Provisions for Financial Bills
All Money Bills are Financial Bills,but vice versa is not true.
Procedure of financial bill is same as ordinary bill, except that financial bill can be introduced only in Lok Sabha and with prior recommendation of President.
Article 118: Rules of Procedure
Each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating its procedure and conduct of business.
Article 119: Regulation of Procedure for Financial Business
Parliament can regulate laws related to financial procedures.
Article 120: Language to be Used in Parliament
Business of Parliament shall be transacted in Hindi or in English.
Unless Parliament by law provides, Use of 'English' to be removed after 15 years.
Presiding officer may allow any member to express themselves in their mother tongue.
Article 121: Restriction on Discussion in Parliament
No discussions shall take place in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court.
Article 122: Court not to Inquire into Proceedings of
No court shall inquire into Parliament proceedings.
Conduct of MPs or officers not subject to court jurisdiction.
Article 123: Power of President to Promulgate Ordinances during Recess President can issue ordinances when both Houses are or even one House is not in session.
Ordinance has same force as an Act of Parliament.
(a) Must be laid before both Houses for their approval & shall cease to operate if not approved after 6 weeks from reassembly unless approved. (Hence Max life if not approved: 6 Months & 6 weeks).
(b) Can be withdrawn anytime by the President.
Cooper v. Union of India Case (1970) - The SC held that the President's satisfaction can be questioned in a court on the grounds of malafide.
Ordinance should not contain provisions beyond Parliament's legislative competence (i.e. on the subjects of union list.)
Ordinance power of President (Centre) under Article 123
Ordinance power of Governor (State) under Article 213.
DC Wadhwa Case vs State of Bihar, 1986: Relates to misuse and repeated re-promulgation of ordinances.
Special Powers of Rajya Sabha 1. Can authorise Parliament to create a new All India Service (Article 312) (Currently 3 - IAS, IPS, IFoS).
2. Can authorise the Parliament to make a law on a Subject of State List. (Article 249)

All these matters are dealt by rules of two houses.

Public Accounts Committee: (PAC)
Established in 1921 through GOI Act 1919.
Total members: 22 members (15 from LS + 7 from RS).
Guide and Philosopher: CAG (submits reports which are analysed by PAC).
Function: To examine the audit reports of CAG.
Estimates Committee:
Established in 1921.
Re-established post Independence: 1950 on recommen- dation of John Mathai Committee.
Total members: 30 (all from LS), (increased from 25 to 30 in 1956).
Function: To examine estimates included in budget Committee on Public Undertakings:
Established in: 1964 on recommendation of Krishna Menon Committee.
Total members: 22 Members (15 from LS + 7 from RS)
(Increased from 15 to 22 in 1974)
Chairman is from Lok Sabha.
Function: To examine reports and accounts of Public Undertakings.
Similar features of all the Financial Committees:
Election: Proportional representation + STV (Single transferable vote)
Appointed/elected by the House or nominated by Speaker/Chairman.
Term of members: 1 year
No Minister can be a member. (Only private member)
